messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard deviation (standard error) of the sampling distribution of the sample mean**

For a one‑sample \(t\)-test, the standard error of the mean (SEM) under the null hypothesis is calculated as:

\[
\text{SEM} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
\(s\) = sample standard deviation = **1.4**  
\(n\) = sample size = **40**

\[
\text{SEM} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.2215
\]

So, the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test (i.e., the standard error of the mean) is approximately **0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis. Standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention population mean of 98.6. For a one-sample t-test, the standard error uses sample standard deviation. So SE = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That is indeed the standard error. So answer: about 0.2215.

Alternatively, if using population standard deviation known? They didn't give population std dev. So use sample std dev.

Thus answer: ~0.2215.

We can also compute t-statistic: (98.2 - 98.6)/SE = -0.4/0.2215 ≈ -1.805. But question only asks for standard deviation of null hypothesis test. So answer: 0.2215.
